quote: We've got a ten ten ten, kilowatt, system.
stewart_read: The customer volunteers a specific system size unprompted — a concrete data point that later becomes the exact reason for disqualification. The rep never reflects it back or treats it as a flag to check before promising a specialist; it's filed silently and only resurfaces as bad news after a hold.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may not have known the 10kW threshold rule at the time it was mentioned, making silent filing a knowledge gap rather than a curiosity-creation failure.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to treat specific numeric disclosures (system size, kWh, bill amount) as immediate checkpoints — flag or verify sizing rules before setting expectations with the customer about a specialist call.

quote: our power goes off quite often.
stewart_read: This is the customer's core pain point — frequent outages in a rural area with unreliable lines — functionally equivalent to a bill-pain anchor for this backup-focused lead. The rep never acknowledges the inconvenience or hardship before pivoting to procedural questions about contracts and prior quotes.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged this detail as background color rather than an anchor since the call was heading toward a specialist handoff regardless.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to verbally acknowledge lived pain ("that's got to be frustrating, losing power regularly") before moving to qualifying questions — it costs seconds and builds the relational credit needed if a DQ has to be delivered later.

quote: Okay. I already talked to somebody about and they gave me a quote. So I I don't know. This is kinda duplicative.
stewart_read: Customer discloses a prior Ion quote he found too expensive. The rep's follow-up ("did you like that quote or not really?") gets a partial answer ("It was on the high side") but the rep never asks who quoted it, when, or what was included — competitive/internal intel that would help avoid redundant outreach or correctly price-anchor a callback.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have been intentionally keeping the call short since the customer's tone suggested fatigue with repeat contact, prioritizing a quick resolution over deeper probing.
coaching_implication: When a customer says a prior quote was duplicative or high, the rep should capture at minimum the ballpark number and rough timeframe — this is free intel for whoever handles the account next and helps prevent Ion re-quoting cold each time.

stewart_read: This is an orphaned-flow, backup-only scenario the rep never ran through the standard orphaned_flow question set (no clean confirmation of owned-vs-leased status beyond an incidental SolarCity mention, no explicit "is your system working" check). Instead of working the qualifying questions first, the rep went straight to a hold to consult a supervisor, and returned with a DQ reason (system too large for battery) that was never verified against the customer directly.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have correctly recognized early that a 10kW existing system with no add-on capacity was outside standard scope and used the hold efficiently rather than wasting call time on a doomed qualification script.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to complete the orphaned_flow question sequence (ownership, working status, panel size) BEFOR going to hold — this either surfaces the DQ reason faster without a hold, or gives the specialist better information when consulted.

quote: our power goes off quite often. We're, in a rural residential area, so, we're susceptible to having the lines go down.
stewart_read: This is the single clearest emotional anchor on the call — recurring outages tied to a specific, named cause (rural lines going down) — functioning like a bill-pain equivalent for a backup-focused lead. The rep never reflects this back as the reason backup power matters, and when the DQ came later, there was no bridge acknowledging that the underlying pain (outages) remains unresolved for the customer.
alternative_hypothesis: Since the call ended in disqualification regardless, using this pain point may not have changed the outcome, making the miss lower-stakes than a live, salvageable lead.
coaching_implication: Even on a call that DQs, closing the loop on the customer's stated pain ("I know the outages are the real issue — I wish I had another option for you") maintains goodwill and keeps the door open for a future non-battery solution if one exists.

quote: they they said your your kilowatt size is too big, and it's too big for a battery or a backup.
stewart_read: The rep did not know battery/backup sizing eligibility rules and had to escalate via a nearly one-minute hold to get an answer, then delivered it as a flat DQ without exploring whether any alternative product exists. Whether alternative backup options exist for oversized systems is not established in the schema or transcript, so this should be flagged as an open question rather than an assumed missed offer.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have handled this appropriately given genuine unfamiliarity with backup-sizing thresholds, and escalating to a specialist rather than guessing is the correct protocol move.
coaching_implication: Flag for Kenny: does Ion have any alternative backup/battery product for oversized existing systems, or is 10kW+ a hard ceiling? If a hard ceiling, equip setters with this threshold up front so holds aren't needed; if alternatives exist, coach reps to offer them before closing out the call.
